summary: A passage from a fiction book (Book 15, part 122) follows Corporal James Rodriguez at the Front Office Bar, a sports-themed upscale bar on the Garden, during the second day of Operation Bogeyman. Rodriguez, now a covert operative affiliated with the CIU, grows disturbed by the mission guidelines given by Commander Marlowe, whom he suspects of madness or of not fully believing his own claims. The passage also contrasts the bar's businessmen clientele with colonists for New Holyoke and notes Rodriguez's lifelong sense of living within rigid lines.
one_line: Corporal James Rodriguez, now a covert operative, doubts the sanity of Operation Bogeyman's guidelines while drinking at a sports-themed bar on the Garden.
key_facts: The Front Office Bar is a themed bar where waitstaff and bartenders dress like sporting referees.
The bar's floor is sectioned into quadrants simulating basketball courts, a baseball infield, the fifty yard line of a domed stadium, and a goalie's crease.
The Front Office Bar caters to young, largely unattached but financially prosperous businessmen on the Garden.
The narrator says the bar's clientele are not colonists for New Holyoke but gentlemen travelling with contracts and deals on their minds.
The passage describes Wall Street-style data snooping for profit, noting that in backwards nations this is called blackmail while on Wall Street it is just called business.
The scene takes place on the second day of Operation Bogeyman.
Corporal James Rodriguez is a former member of the 15th Marine Frontier Expeditionary Force, C Company, and is now a CIU affiliated covert operative.
Rodriguez did not finish his degree at Virginia Tech.
Rodriguez finds the mission guidelines psychotic and hopes his misperception of them is the explanation.
Rodriguez is unsure whether Commander Marlowe actually believes the mission rationale he presents.
Commander Marlowe claims to have experienced an event that others connect to the current operation, which seems to irritate Marlowe.
The Semper Opera House is located next to where Diana lives.
Rodriguez has spent his whole life inside parental, social, procedural, martial and racial lines.
The passage opens with a wordless moment in which Diana takes Rodriguez's hand and walks with shoulders touching, conveying that everything between them is fine.
